{"id": "96:8/q02", "question": "Who is addressed by 'your Lord,' and what does the address do?", "turns_on": "Whether the rhetorical shift addresses the human directly or the sequence of preceding addresses continues to address the Prophet.", "positions": [{"id": "96:8/q02/p1", "position": "The human being, especially the transgressor, is addressed directly as a warning.", "reasons": "Kashshāf, Rāzī, Bayḍāwī, and Nasafī call the turn to direct address a threat about transgression; ʿAlūsī and Ṭabāṭabāʾī report this as an emphatic shift, although they prefer the Prophet as addressee."}, {"id": "96:8/q02/p2", "position": "The Prophet is addressed, while the transgressor is warned and the Prophet consoled.", "reasons": "ʿAlūsī and Ṭabāṭabāʾī prefer this because preceding addresses are to the Prophet. {"id": "96:8/q04", "question": "What does al-rujʿā mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the verbal expression names the act of return or its endpoint; several sources allow both.", "positions": [{"id": "96:8/q04/p1", "position": "The act of returning.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda and al-Akhfash are reported by Wāḥidī; Wāḥidī equates it with rujūʿan and marjiʿan. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports this majority gloss."}, {"id": "96:8/q04/p2", "position": "The place, endpoint, or ultimate destination of return.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda allows the place as well as the act. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk, as transmitted by Māwardī, calls it the final destination; Ibn al-Jawzī and Rāzī also give destination or place. {"id": "96:8/q05", "question": "What is the form and syntactic case of al-rujʿā?", "turns_on": "The notes treat form and case as compatible analyses, while differing in their reported pattern labels.", "positions": [{"id": "96:8/q05/p1", "position": "It is a verbal noun on a fuʿlā or faʿlā type pattern, with a feminine final alif.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī calls it faʿlā; Baghawī and Qurṭubī give a faʿlā/faʿla description. The sources' pattern labels vary while sharing a verbal-noun analysis."}, {"id": "96:8/q05/p2", "position": "Its syntactic position is accusative, although the final alif hides the case ending.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās states the underlying case and the reason it cannot be heard."}]}

{"id": "96:8/q07", "question": "What reading and codex-spelling observations are supplied?", "turns_on": "Whether atypical codex forms have sound orthographic reasons or are writing mistakes; none of these notes ties an alternative spelling to this verse.", "positions": [{"id": "96:8/q07/p1", "position": "One reported choice concerns a hāʾ's vowel: both forms are sound, but ḍamma is preferred as more regular.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī reports al-Taysīr accepting both and al-Kāfī preferring ḍamma; he also prefers ḍamma because Ḥamza uses it where preceding yāʾ derives from alif. He regards most orthographic departures as purposeful or analogical. A report attributes to ʿUthmān the claim that Arabs would correct errors orally; al-Dānī rejects it because ʿUthmān would not leave baseless errors to repair."}, {"id": "96:8/q07/p3", "position": "The reported attribution to ʿUthmān that Arabs would correct codex errors orally is rejected.", "reasons": "Al-Dānī says leaving such errors would make writing pointless and burdensome; Ibn al-Jazarī instead expects a sound rationale in early spelling."}]}
{"id": "96:8/q08", "question": "When and in what sense does the return to God occur?", "turns_on": "Whether return is restricted to the afterlife, includes reversals and dependence in worldly life, also evokes origin, or is read inwardly as self-annihilation.", "positions": [{"id": "96:8/q08/p1", "position": "It is the return after death for resurrection, gathering, judgment, and recompense.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī says Muhammad's opponent will taste intolerable punishment; Wāḥidī, Qurṭubī, and Nasafī stress requital for tyranny. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says resurrection and gathering diminish worldly wealth; Abū Ḥayyān adds reckoning. Rāzī cites 14:42–43 for deferred punishment and says the warning benefits the steadfast more than pleasure-seekers. Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 78:21–22 for Hell and 84:6 for universal return. Islahi says neglected lordship and divine power will become plain. Kurdish? No: Kur'an Yolu calls it the first Hereafter allusion if this is the first sūra, citing 2:177 and 4:136 for later explicit accountability."}, {"id": "96:8/q08/p2", "position": "God also returns people in this life from maturity, wealth, and strength to weakness, poverty, decline, and death.", "reasons": "Māwardī mentions maturity to decline and life to death; Rāzī makes the reversal symmetrical with God's earlier raising from inertness to life, poverty to wealth, and lowliness to honor."}, {"id": "96:8/q08/p3", "position": "Return embraces present dependence on God's decree as well as the final judgment after death.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī says no one acts in worldly life except by God's decree and all deeds receive fitting reward or punishment later, citing 95:7–8 in the full version. Ibn ʿĀshūr adds that wealth never removes dependence on God or knowledge of one's fate; return can metaphorically suggest need of the one returned to."}, {"id": "96:8/q08/p4", "position": "All existence returns to God as its source as well as returning for judgment.", "reasons": "Asad gives both senses; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ connects human origin in a clot with God as beginning and end and cites 92:13."}, {"id": "96:8/q08/p5", "position": "Inwardly, return is the annihilation of the self's essence and attributes before the true divine actor.", "reasons": "Qāshānī relates this to the Prophet's humble statement that he is not the reader: God is the true reader."}]}
{"id": "96:8/q09", "question": "Who returns to God?", "turns_on": "Whether the local threat is read through the Abū Jahl reports or through the generic human described in the preceding creation and transgression verses; universal return is also asserted.", "positions": [{"id": "96:8/q09/p1", "position": "All people or all creation return, whatever their wealth, conduct, or rank.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī and Bursawī say all return at death and resurrection. Quṭb lists righteous and wicked, obedient and disobedient, rich and poor; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 84:6. Biqāʿī says all are dependent in life and death."}, {"id": "96:8/q09/p2", "position": "The immediate warning targets the self-sufficient transgressor, exemplified by Abū Jahl.", "reasons": "Muqātil identifies Abū Jahl using 96:15–16's forelock; Ṭabarī calls him Muhammad's opponent. Elmalılı mentions the arrogant unbeliever of the revelation occasion; ʿAlūsī says the Prophet can be addressed while the tyrant is warned."}, {"id": "96:8/q09/p3", "position": "The surface context concerns the generic human, though reports point more readily to Abū Jahl.", "reasons": "Rāzī prefers humanity generally: after creation, blessing, and enrichment, people sin and pursue appetite, yet face judgment. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports his solution and extends the pattern to forgetting return and forbidding worship. Ibn ʿĀshūr assigns the general transgression statement through 96:8 a preparatory role for the specific Abū Jahl episode from 96:9."}]}

Bursawī's Persian couplet says deeds last after wealth passes."}]}
{"id": "96:8/q11", "question": "How does the verse connect to its surrounding passage and other verses?", "turns_on": "The notes offer complementary links: nearby transgression, the sūra's knowledge and wealth contrast, and the wider creation-to-return arc.", "positions": [{"id": "96:8/q11/p1", "position": "It carries the warning from human enrichment and transgression into the specific prayer-forbidding tyrant episode.", "reasons": "Muqātil links the warning about Abū Jahl to the forelock in 96:15–16. {"id": "96:8/q12", "question": "What is reported about Abū Jahl's request for Mecca's mountains?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "96:8/q12/p1", "position": "Abū Jahl proposed turning the mountains to gold and silver; Gabriel offered it with a severe warning, and the Prophet withheld the prayer to spare them.", "reasons": "Rāzī's two versions say riches would make the Quraysh transgress, leave their religion, and follow Muhammad; they differ in citing 5:115 and 5:112 for the table punishment. {"id": "96:8/q13", "question": "What other transmitted sayings illustrate knowledge, wealth, and return?", "turns_on": "The notes transmit two different sayings for the same moral contrast.", "positions": [{"id": "96:8/q13/p1", "position": "Two seekers are never satisfied: the seeker of knowledge and the seeker of worldly gain.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr says it was transmitted as a Prophetic report; Bursawī attributes it to Ibn Masʿūd and adds that knowledge increases divine favor whereas world-seeking increases rebellion."}, {"id": "96:8/q13/p2", "position": "The Prophet sought refuge from wealth that causes tyranny and poverty that causes forgetfulness.", "reasons": "Bursawī reports this prayer as part of the knowledge and wealth contrast."}]}
{"id": "96:8/q14", "question": "What inward error makes people imagine themselves independent of the Lord?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "96:8/q14/p1", "position": "People mistake entrusted divine names and attributes manifested within them for their own possessions and become proud.", "reasons": "Bursawī says these manifestations should instead be recognized as signs of their Creator and of continued dependence on Him."}]}
{"id": "96:8/q15", "question": "What sūra facts and chronology are reported?", "turns_on": "The chronology turns on whether the prayer passage belongs immediately after the first five revelations, given the reported later start of obligatory prayer.", "positions": [{"id": "96:8/q15/p1", "position": "The sūra is Meccan and has seventeen verses.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī states both particulars."}, {"id": "96:8/q15/p2", "position": "Whether these verses followed the first five immediately is disputed.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr reports that mention of prayer seems difficult if obligatory prayer began years later at the Night Journey; some place intervening revelation and later attachment, while others deny the first five were the earliest revelation."}, {"id": "96:8/q15/p3", "position": "If al-ʿAlaq was the first sūra, this is the Quran's first allusion to the Hereafter.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu attributes this conditional conclusion to those accepting the first-sūra premise and contrasts later explicit statements of accountability, citing 2:177 and 4:136."}, {"id": "96:8/q15/p4", "position": "Reciting this sūra earns a reward like reciting the whole set of shorter sūras.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī transmits this as a Prophetic report."}]}
{"id": "96:8/q16", "question": "How is the earlier rebuke kalla related to this warning?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "96:8/q16/p1", "position": "Kalla anticipates and rebukes the later description of one who forbids a servant's prayer.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says kalla normally follows the speech it rejects; its initial placement here points forward to the target in 96:9 and following, and he compares an initial negative particle in Imru al-Qays."}]}
{"id": "96:9/q01", "question": "What does 'Have you seen?' express?", "turns_on": "Whether the question conveys wonder, inquiry, warning or the later moral contrast.", "positions": [{"id": "96:9/q01/p1", "position": "It draws attention to the astonishing impropriety of forbidding worship.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī and Baghawī say repetition intensifies wonder. Rāzī highlights the irony of Abū al-Ḥakam, an idol worshipper who forbids his Creator's service, and recalls the Prophet's prayer for Abū Jahl or ʿUmar. Ibn ʿĀshūr compares the extraordinary-event question at 88:1; Qutb hears a rapid live address."}, {"id": "96:9/q01/p2", "position": "It contrasts the guided, pious worshipper with the denying, turning preventer and God's seeing both.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, Baghawī and al-Kashshāf develop this contrast. Al-Ālūsī offers an escalating sequence from general prevention to claimed guidance to actual denial; the majority's contrast is broader. ʿIṣām al-Dīn makes a more elaborate sequence from tyranny to lost guidance to earned punishment, which al-Ālūsī calls far-fetched."}, {"id": "96:9/q01/p3", "position": "It means 'tell me' or 'inform me', using sight as an image of certain knowledge.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī explains inward clarity through seeing; al-Rāghib compares the interrogative with akhbirnī. Qurṭubī supplies whether he is safe from punishment. Ibn Kathīr calls the first rebuke gentle."}]}
{"id": "96:9/q02", "question": "How are the repeated interrogatives and omissions parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether raʾayta takes a second object, whether a conditional can fill it, and whether an interrogative apodosis needs fāʾ.", "positions": [{"id": "96:9/q02/p1", "position": "The first question takes the prohibitor as object, later objects are omitted, and the final interrogative supplies the threatening complement.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān requires the second object to be an interrogative clause, citing 53:33–35, 19:77–78, 56:58–59. Al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī call the omissions contextual rather than tanāzuʿ because whole clauses do not compete as omitted individual words. Ibn ʿĀshūr supplies the answer from 96:14."}, {"id": "96:9/q02/p2", "position": "The relative clause and a conditional are two objects of the first question; the middle question is emphatic and the later answer supplies the first missing answer.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī's parse is transmitted by Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn and held by al-Naṣafī. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Raḍī allow an interrogative answer without fāʾ, citing 6:47; Abū Ḥayyān, al-Damāmīnī, al-Samīn and Bint al-Shāṭiʾ object that fāʾ is required."}, {"id": "96:9/q02/p3", "position": "Three linked challenges have their expansive omitted conclusions compressed into the last question.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says one concise threat completes all three; al-Ṭabarī calls the repetitions substitutions, making the forbidding and denying man answerable to God's sight."}, {"id": "96:9/q02/p4", "position": "The first question may be visual and the later ones cognitive, with conditional answers supplied at the end.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this mixed analysis and another in which all three are cognitive; unjoining the last clause marks its independent threatening force."}, {"id": "96:9/q02/p5", "position": "The interrogative is a stylistic prompt that need not take any inferred second object.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ cites analogous Meccan questions at 107:1, 19:77, 25:43, 45:23, 53:33 and 56:58, 63, 68, 71, resisting speculative grammatical complements."}, {"id": "96:9/q02/p6", "position": "As a challenge rather than cognitive vision, it does not take two objects.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya distinguishes it from knowledge-based seeing."}]}
